Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Robert, a 51-year-old school principal, had always prided himself on his steady composure and robust health, a bedrock that allowed him to navigate the daily demands of his busy school and the quiet grief of his late wife’s passing. That bedrock shattered two years ago when a sudden, aggressive infection spiraled into acute sepsis, leading to a frantic emergency room visit and an extended stay in the intensive care unit. He remembered the blinding fluorescent lights, the constant beeping, the cold, metallic smell of the hospital that seemed to permeate everything. He remembered the feeling of utter powerlessness as his body, which he had always trusted, fought a battle he couldn't comprehend, tubes and wires his only companions. He lay there, his system overwhelmed, convinced he was dying, his very being reduced to a fragile, failing machine.

Now, two years later, the memory of that time was a strange, fragmented thing. When he tried to deliberately recall the details of his ICU stay, the specifics often eluded him, a jumble of blurred images and disjointed sensations. Yet, a sudden whiff of alcohol, perhaps from the hand sanitizer a teacher used in the hallway, or the antiseptic spray from the school nurse’s office, could instantly transport him back. In those moments, a wave of intense fear would wash over him, his heart pounding, his breath catching, the terror palpable even without a clear picture of what caused it. Sometimes, an unexpected sensation would grip him – a tightness in his chest, a peculiar pressure in his limbs – making him feel as though his body was once again pinned to that hospital bed, tubes snaking from every orifice, reliving the frightening stillness of being critically ill.

Robert found himself constantly vigilant, his world shrinking. The scent of antiseptic, so common in a school environment, became a constant threat, causing him to take circuitous routes around the nurse's office or avoid certain cleaning supplies. The very idea of a medical examination, even a routine check-up, filled him with an overwhelming dread. He had missed his last two annual physicals, crucial for his employment, inventing increasingly elaborate excuses. He was certain that his body was fundamentally unreliable, a ticking time bomb waiting to betray him again. This belief extended to his very self; he had come to believe that he could no longer rely on himself to manage his responsibilities, to make sound decisions. The confident, capable principal he once was seemed to have vanished, replaced by a man he barely recognised, perpetually on edge.

To manage this pervasive unease, Robert had developed a series of rigid routines. Every conversation, from a simple exchange with a student to a complex meeting with a parent or a teacher, was meticulously rehearsed in his head multiple times beforehand. He’d anticipate every possible question, every potential response, desperate to avoid any misstep that might expose his perceived incompetence. This constant mental preparation left him exhausted, and he found himself pulling away from others. He stopped attending faculty social events, declined invitations from old friends, and even started eating lunch alone in his office, claiming paperwork. He had effectively cut off almost all contact with his friends and family, isolating himself completely in his carefully constructed bubble of predictability.

The consequences of his isolation were beginning to weigh heavily. His colleagues, once accustomed to his approachable demeanor, now found him distant and preoccupied. His assistant had gently inquired about his missed physicals, a clear indication that his avoidance was becoming noticeable. What frightened him most was the possibility that his carefully maintained facade might crumble, exposing the fragile, unreliable man he felt himself to be. It was this fear, coupled with the sheer exhaustion of living in constant apprehension, that finally brought Robert to seek help, hoping to find a way back to the man he once was, or at least to a version of himself he could recognise and trust.
